title: Stage 8, Lesson 3: The 4% rule - how much to draw from a retirement pot without running out
subtitle: A classic rule for estimating how much you can withdraw each year in retirement without running dry halfway through.
whyItMatters: This rule answers the question that matters most in retirement planning - "how much do I need to retire safely?" - by turning a vague question into a number you can actually calculate.
openingQuestion: What does the 4% rule say about drawing money from a retirement pot?
openingOptions: Draw exactly 4% of your total assets every month, steadily, throughout the whole of a long retirement
Draw 4% in the first year, then adjust that amount for inflation each year
Draw 4% of whatever balance is left each year, so the absolute figure naturally falls over time as it is used
You are only permitted to draw exactly 4% once, right at the moment you formally enter retirement
explanation: The 4% rule (from the Trinity Study): draw 4% of the portfolio in the first year of retirement, then in later years adjust that amount for inflation - not recompute 4% on the new balance. With a sensibly balanced stock/bond portfolio, this has had a high historical success rate at sustaining the pot for at least 30 years.

diagram.label: Draw 4% of the portfolio in year one
Adjust that amount for inflation in later years
Do not recompute 4% on the new balance

realWorldExample.description: The Trinity Study looked at historical US market data and found that a 4%-a-year withdrawal rate, adjusted for inflation, had a very high probability of sustaining a retirement pot for at least 30 years - which is how it became the most widely cited reference point in personal retirement planning.

quiz.question: If your retirement pot is 6 billion dong when you retire, roughly how much can you draw in the first year under the 4% rule?
options: 240 million in the first month
240 million (4% of 6 billion)
600 million (10% of 6 billion)
24 million (0.4% of 6 billion)
quiz.explanation: 4% × 6 billion = 240 million in the first year. In later years that amount rises with inflation (at 3% inflation you would draw about 247 million the following year) rather than being recomputed as 4% of the new balance, which may be higher or lower depending on the market.

quiz.question: Why is the 4% rule not an absolute 100% guarantee but only a high-probability estimate?
options: Because the rule has never been tested against any data
Because regulators can change the 4% figure at any time
Because future market performance does not repeat the past
Because the 4% rule only holds for an all-bond portfolio
quiz.explanation: The 4% rule rests on historical data, not on a mathematical guarantee about the future. The biggest danger is sequence of returns risk - if the market falls sharply in the first few years of retirement, drawing steadily from a shrinking portfolio can empty it faster than planned.

quiz.question: After drawing 4% in year one, how is the amount for later years worked out?
options: Draw out the whole of whatever profit the portfolio earned over the past year
Recompute 4% of the portfolio value at the start of each new financial year
Draw 4% more than the amount that was drawn in the immediately preceding year
Keep the year-one amount and adjust it for inflation each year
quiz.explanation: The aim is to hold purchasing power steady, not to hold the percentage steady. Recomputing 4% every year sounds safer but makes your standard of living swing with the market - which retirees find hard to live with.

quiz.question: Over what period was the 4% rule tested?
options: Thirty years, matching a typical retirement beginning at sixty
Ten years, enough to cover one average economic cycle in the market
The whole of the rest of a person's life, with no specific number of years
Fifty years, so that it also suits people who retire extremely early
quiz.explanation: Thirty years is the central assumption of the Trinity Study. That is why someone retiring at 45, or someone with a long life expectancy, needs a lower withdrawal rate - their horizon is different.

quiz.question: What can cause the 4% rule to fail?
options: Inflation staying low throughout the whole of that person's retirement
A run of sharp falls right at the start of retirement, just as withdrawals begin
The market growing faster than its average rate over the first twenty years
The retiree spending less than the plan originally assumed they would
quiz.explanation: Withdrawing from a falling portfolio sells more units, and those units are not there to recover. At the same average return, the order of the years decides whether you run out.

quiz.question: Which piece of flexibility lowers the risk for a retiree?
options: Moving the whole portfolio into cash the moment the market starts falling
Raising the withdrawal in a falling year to make up for the value that was lost
Trimming the withdrawal in badly falling years where spending allows it
Holding the withdrawal steady whatever the market does so the plan stays intact
quiz.explanation: Cutting spending by 10% through two bad years improves the success probability of the whole plan considerably. The 4% rule is a starting point, not a contract - flexibility is the strongest variable you control.

keyTakeaways: The 4% rule: draw 4% of the portfolio in year one, then adjust for inflation each year - do not recompute the percentage on the new balance
Built on historical data (the Trinity Study), it carries a high success probability but is not an absolute guarantee
The biggest risk is a sharp market fall right at the start of retirement (sequence of returns risk)

practicePrompt.question: You retire with a 5 billion portfolio, apply the 4% rule and draw 200 million in year one. In year two the market falls sharply and the portfolio is down to 4 billion. Should you recompute 4% on the new balance (4 billion) and draw 160 million?
options: No - adjust the original 200 million for inflation instead of recomputing 4% on the new balance
Yes, recompute exactly 4% on the new balance each year so the withdrawal rate stays consistent whether the portfolio rises or falls
You should draw more than 200 million that year to make up for the value the portfolio lost over the previous year
You should stop withdrawing altogether during a falling year and only resume once the portfolio recovers to its original level
practicePrompt.explanation: The 4% rule adjusts the absolute amount for inflation each year rather than recomputing the percentage against the new portfolio value - the distinction people most often get wrong.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than as a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Work it out now
application.message: Take the invested assets you expect to hold at retirement and multiply by 4% - that is what you can draw in year one, with later years only adjusted for inflation.
application.secondary: This is a starting estimate, not a fixed and final figure.

sections.text: Once you have accumulated enough to retire, the next question is: how much should you draw each year so that it is enough to live on without emptying the pot halfway through? The 4% withdrawal rule, out of the Trinity Study, is the classic answer.

In the first year of retirement you draw 4% of the portfolio. If your pot is 6 billion dong, year one is 4% × 6 billion = 240 million. The part that is easiest to misread: from year two onwards you do NOT recompute 4% of the new balance, which may be higher or lower depending on the market - you simply adjust that 240 million for inflation. If inflation is 3% that year, you draw around 247 million the next year, whether your pot rose or fell.

The Trinity Study worked through historical US market data across many different periods, bad ones included, and found that a 4%-a-year withdrawal adjusted for inflation had a very high probability of sustaining the pot for at least 30 years with a sensibly balanced stock/bond portfolio. Drawing more, say 6-8%, raises the risk of the pot running out before you do by a wide margin.
The biggest risk: a market fall right at the start of retirement

The 4% rule is not an absolute mathematical guarantee, because future market performance will not be an exact copy of the past. The most dangerous risk is called sequence of returns risk: if the market falls hard in the first few years of retirement, having to keep drawing while the portfolio is shrinking erodes it far faster than the same fall would have done in year 20.

items: Draw 4% of the portfolio in the first year of retirement, then adjust only for inflation - do not recompute the percentage on the new balance
Consider drawing less than 4% (3-3.5%, say) if you want more safety or expect to retire early and live off the pot for longer than 30 years
Keep part of the portfolio in less volatile assets (bonds, cash) so you are not forced to sell equities exactly while the market is falling

lines: 4% is a starting point for planning, not a sacred number - adjust it to the circumstances you actually have.
